query: For high-entropy-alloy materials intended for self-lubricating moving components, what single intervention could reduce both coefficient of friction and wear rate across a wide service-temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites prior evidence supporting it, and proposes an experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled thermal oxidation treatment that promotes the in-situ formation of a nanostructured oxide glaze layer on the HEA surface will simultaneously reduce the coefficient of friction and wear rate over a wide service-temperature range compared to the untreated material.
generation.material_initial_state: Untreated CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy with a conventional microstructure and native surface oxides.
generation.intervention: A single-step thermal oxidation treatment (e.g., annealing at approximately 800°C for 1 hour) designed to convert the top surface into a continuous, self-adaptive oxide glaze layer.
generation.conditions: Tribological testing under sliding conditions across a broad temperature range (from ambient up to 600–800°C) and under varied normal loads representative of industrial or automotive applications.
generation.structural_mediator: A dense, nanostructured oxide glaze layer that is self-healing and provides solid lubrication.
generation.mechanism: The controlled thermal oxidation modifies the surface by forming a lubricious oxide glaze that minimizes adhesive wear and reduces abrasive damage. This layer acts as a protective barrier, lowering the shear stress at the contact interface and thereby decreasing both friction and material loss during sliding.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the untreated alloy (which typically exhibits a friction coefficient around 0.3 and higher wear rates), the treated HEA is expected to achieve a markedly lower friction coefficient (potentially reducing it to below 0.1) and a significantly lower wear rate across the tested temperature range.
generation.baseline: The performance metrics (friction coefficient and wear rate) of the untreated HEA under similar sliding conditions and temperature regimes.
generation.boundary: The intervention is expected to remain effective as long as the thermal oxidation treatment parameters are optimized to form a uniform glaze layer. Deviations from optimal annealing temperatures or times might lead to discontinuous or brittle oxide layers that could compromise tribological performance.
generation.uncertainty: While early evidence supports the formation of lubricious oxide layers under thermal treatment, the long-term stability and quantitative improvements across extreme cyclic temperature conditions remain to be fully established.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of CoCrFeMnNi HEA samples: one set undergoes the controlled thermal oxidation treatment (anneal at ~800°C for 1h) while the other set remains untreated. Subject both sets to standardized sliding wear tests under controlled normal loads and across a temperature range from ambient up to 600–800°C. Characterize the surface layers pre- and post-testing using SEM and EDS, and record friction coefficients and wear rates.
measurements: Coefficient of friction during sliding tests
Wear rate (volume loss per unit load and distance)
Thickness and integrity of the oxide glaze layer
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated samples do not demonstrate a statistically significant reduction in both the friction coefficient and wear rate across the entire tested temperature range relative to the untreated samples, or if the oxide layer proves unstable under operational conditions, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

AbstractAlCrTiZrMo high-entropy alloy (HEA) films with strong amorphization were obtained by co-filter cathode vacuum arc deposition, and the effect of thermal shock on the films was investigated in order to explore the protection mechanism of HEA films against mechanical components in extreme service environments. The results show that after annealing at 800 °C for 1 h, the formation of a dense ZrTiO4 composite oxide layer on the surface actively prevents the oxidation from continuing, so that the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film exhibits excellent oxidation resistance at 800 °C in air. In the friction-corrosion coupling environment, the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film annealed at 800 °C for 1 h shows the best tribocorrosion resistance due to the stable dense microstructure and excellent mechanical properties, and its ΔOCP, COF and wear rate possess the smallest values of 0.055, 0.04 and 1.34 × 10−6 mm−3·N−1·m−1.Keywords: AlCrTiZrMo high-entropy alloy film, thermal shock, oxidation, tribocorrosion

frame.system: High-entropy alloy (HEA) used for self-lubricating moving components, currently in an untreated state characterized by conventional microstructure and standard surface chemistry.
frame.goal: Reduce both the coefficient of friction and wear rate over a wide service-temperature range using a single, unified intervention.
frame.limitation: Current HEA systems or previous treatments tend to offer limited performance improvements—often addressing only friction or wear and typically effective within a narrow temperature window. This leaves a gap in achieving robust tribological properties across diverse operational conditions.
root_cause_cues: reduce both coefficient of friction and wear rate
constraints: Only one intervention is allowed (i.e. a single processing or compositional modification step)
The intervention must be effective across a broad range of service temperatures
It must simultaneously lower friction and wear without compromising other material properties
frame.regime: Tribological testing under conditions spanning low to high temperatures, representative of the operational environment of moving components (e.g., from ambient up to elevated temperatures encountered in industrial or automotive applications).
prior_attempts: Alloying with multiple phases or adding separate solid lubricants (e.g., MoS2, graphene) in multi-step processes, which often enhanced either friction reduction or wear resistance but not both simultaneously or not consistently across the full temperature range.

decision.trend: Early studies on HEA tribological performance focused on tailoring the microstructure to achieve low friction and wear—for example, demonstrating that dynamic surface amorphization (PMC7311485) and nanohierarchical architectures with composition undulation (PMC10241162) could significantly reduce wear at room and moderately elevated temperatures. Subsequent work introduced processing methods (such as thermal shock and annealing) that developed dense, protective oxide layers on HEA film surfaces (PMC10456374), and even the use of 2D HEA nanoflakes which, through tribocatalytic activity, produced extremely low friction and wear under high contact pressures (PMC12019924). These approaches have incrementally moved from solely tuning bulk microstructure to actively engineering the surface/interface to respond dynamically, but none has yet provided a single-step method that robustly addresses both friction and wear reduction across a very wide temperature range.
decision.unsolved: A persistent challenge is to obtain a unified, single-step intervention that induces an adaptive, self-lubricating surface across a broad service-temperature spectrum. In previous methods, either only friction or wear was addressed, or the effect was limited to a narrow temperature window. The key unsolved issue is using one treatment to consistently create a surface that not only reduces friction but also minimizes wear, and that maintains these properties from ambient up to high temperatures.
decision.lever: Develop a controlled thermal oxidation treatment that converts the top surface of the untreated HEA into a self-adaptive, nanostructured oxide glaze layer
decision.why: Building on the trend where both microstructure modification and surface oxidation (as seen in PMC10456374 and PMC12019924) have individually provided improvements, the most plausible next step is to use a single thermal treatment that forms a robust, lubricious oxide surface. This lever offers a unified intervention that can tailor the surface chemistry and structure to yield a protective, low-shear glaze; the in-situ oxidation is expected to lower the coefficient of friction (potentially from ~0.3 down to below 0.1) and simultaneously reduce wear rate significantly, while being thermodynamically stable and self-healing over a wide temperature range.
